history.hpi: Wife reports three days of productive cough with yellow-green sputum and fever, worsening over the last 24 hours. This morning he became increasingly short of breath and confused, prompting the 911 call.
history.lastOralIntake: Small amount of broth this morning, poor intake overall today
history.events: Wife called 911 after noting worsening confusion and labored breathing over the past hour

scene.location: Single-family home, living room, patient in recliner
scene.bystanders: Wife present, provides history of three days of worsening productive cough and fever
visualCues: Patient slumped in recliner, visibly working to breathe
Productive cough with yellow-green sputum in a nearby tissue
Wife holding a thermometer showing 103.1°F from earlier this morning

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 71-year-old male with three days of worsening productive cough and fever, now hypoxic, tachypneic, confused, and hypotensive, consistent with severe sepsis from a pulmonary source.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses weak and rapid, flash capillary refill
otherFindings: Coarse crackles auscultated at the right lung base

expectedActions.shortAction: Administer supplemental oxygen via non-rebreather targeting SpO2 94-98%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects hypoxia from the pneumonia while workup continues.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish IV access; begin 500 mL isotonic fluid bolus, pressure infused over less than 15 min toward MAP 65 mmHg
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish IV access. IV fluid volume goal attained by giving boluses that are pressure infused over less than 15 minutes each ... Physiologic target: MAP goal 65 mmHg. Fluid goal of up to 30 mL/kg of isotonic fluid by administering rapid, predetermined boluses (e.g., 500 mL) unless the MAP goal is achieved, or pulmonary edema develops
expectedActions.rationale: Volume resuscitation is first-line for septic shock and should generally precede positive-pressure ventilation in a hypotensive patient.

transitions.condition: Crew administers supplemental oxygen targeting 94-98% saturation, establishes IV access, and begins an isotonic fluid bolus toward a MAP goal of 65 mmHg before considering CPAP.

transitions.if: CPAP applied before adequate fluid resuscitation
transitions.condition: Crew applies CPAP for the hypoxia before an adequate fluid bolus has been given, adding positive intrathoracic pressure to an already volume-depleted, hypotensive patient.

phases.name: O2 and IV fluids started
phases.description: Crew begins supplemental oxygen and IV fluid resuscitation for suspected septic shock from a pulmonary source, sequencing fluids before adding positive-pressure support given the patient's hypotension.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew starts supplemental oxygen, establishes IV access, and begins a rapid isotonic fluid bolus toward a MAP goal of 65 mmHg, prioritizing volume resuscitation before escalating to CPAP given the hypotension.

otherFindings: 500 mL isotonic bolus infusing under pressure

expectedActions.shortAction: Norepinephrine infusion 1.7 mcg/min (85 kg × 0.02 mcg/kg/min), titrate to MAP 65 mmHg
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Vasopressors (shock unresponsive to IV fluids) titrated to physiologic targets ... Norepinephrine 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/minute — Preference in both neurogenic and infectious (sepsis) causes of distributive shock
expectedActions.rationale: Norepinephrine is preferred for fluid-refractory septic shock.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply CPAP for persistent hypoxia only after adequate fluid resuscitation and pressor support are underway
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) should be considered early for severe respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure. NIV options include continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
expectedActions.rationale: Sequencing CPAP after volume/pressor support reduces the risk of a sudden preload drop in a hypotensive patient.

transitions.condition: Despite the fluid bolus and oxygen, the patient remains hypotensive and hypoxic; crew starts norepinephrine while carefully adding CPAP for the ongoing hypoxia.

phases.name: Fluid-refractory shock, norepinephrine started
phases.description: With persistent hypotension despite fluids, the crew starts norepinephrine and carefully adds CPAP for the ongoing hypoxia, watching closely for any hemodynamic effect from the added intrathoracic pressure.
phases.triggerCondition: The patient remains hypotensive after the initial fluid bolus; crew starts a norepinephrine infusion for fluid-refractory shock and cautiously applies CPAP for the persistent hypoxia, monitoring blood pressure closely.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess full vital signs and CPAP seal at least every 15 minutes en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Full vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) with reassessment q 15 minutes or more frequently as appropriate
expectedActions.rationale: Ongoing reassessment catches early re-deterioration and ensures the CPAP mask seal is maintained.

transitions.if: Perfusion and oxygenation improve, transport continues
transitions.condition: With fluids, norepinephrine, and CPAP in place, perfusion and oxygenation trend toward normal; crew continues reassessment en route.

phases.name: Perfusion and oxygenation improve, transport continues
phases.description: With combined fluid, pressor, and respiratory support, the patient's perfusion and oxygenation trend toward normal. The crew continues serial reassessment and maintains the CPAP seal throughout transport.
phases.triggerCondition: After norepinephrine titration and continued CPAP, vital signs and mental status improve; crew maintains ongoing reassessment and CPAP seal en route.

otherFindings: Advanced notification given to receiving hospital
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I can breathe a bit easier now."

phases.name: CPAP applied before adequate fluid resuscitation
phases.description: CPAP is applied for the hypoxia before an adequate fluid bolus has been completed. The added positive intrathoracic pressure further reduces preload in this volume-depleted septic patient, worsening hypotension.
phases.triggerCondition: CPAP is started for the ongoing hypoxia before the fluid bolus is complete; the added intrathoracic pressure drops venous return and worsens the existing hypotension.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses weaker than before CPAP
otherFindings: Blood pressure has fallen further since CPAP initiation
Fluid bolus still infusing, not yet complete

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize CPAP-related preload drop; complete fluid resuscitation and reconsider CPAP pressure/pause if hypotension worsens
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Increased intrathoracic pressure can progressively decrease cardiac output and is most notable when PEEP is greater than 15 cmH2O. The higher the level of PEEP (over 5 cmH2O), the more likely the patient will experience a variety of adverse consequences, both ventilatory and hemodynamic
expectedActions.rationale: Positive intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return; in a volume-depleted septic patient this can worsen hypotension unless adequate fluid resuscitation precedes or accompanies it.
